passages.happening:
Agrippa tells Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Paul stretches out his hand and begins his defence (verse 1).

He says he counts himself fortunate to make his defence before King Agrippa against all the accusations of the Jews (verse 2), “especially since you are acquainted with all the Jewish customs and controversies” (verse 3). He asks the king to listen patiently (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
This is Paul's longest defence in Acts, and his last. The setting is grand: the king and Bernice, the governor, the commanders and leading men of the city (25:23). Paul ‘stretched out his hand’, the gesture of a speaker beginning a formal address. His Greek in this speech is some of the most polished in the book.

His opening is courteous, and this time it is sincere. Agrippa II really did know Jewish customs and disputes. Rome had given him oversight of the temple and the right to appoint the high priest (the note on 25:13-21 says more). For once Paul is speaking to a judge who can understand what the argument is about.

‘The accusations of the Jews’ means the charges brought by the leaders in Jerusalem, the high priest and his party, as in the chapters before. The speaker is a Jew, speaking to a Jewish king. The note on Acts 13:42-47 sets out how this site reads such phrases, and it applies to every use of the phrase in this chapter (verses 2, 7 and 21).
passages.ot: Speaking before kings was the calling of Israel's prophets. Moses stood before Pharaoh, Elijah before Ahab, and Daniel before Nebuchadnezzar. The Psalms carry the same hope: “I will speak of Your testimonies before kings, and I will not be ashamed” (Psalm 119:46).
passages.asks: Paul found something true and good to say about the man who would judge him, and said it without flattery. Ask whether you can be honestly courteous to people in power, even when you disagree with them. And ask whether you are ready, as Paul was, to give a full account of your faith when someone is willing to listen.

passages.t: On trial for the hope of Israel
passages.happening:
All the Jews know how Paul has lived since his youth, among his own people and in Jerusalem (verse 4). They can testify, if they are willing, “that I lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest sect of our religion” (verse 5).

“And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise that God made to our fathers” (verse 6), the promise Israel's twelve tribes hope to see fulfilled as they worship God day and night (verse 7). It is for this hope that he is accused (verse 7). “Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Paul presents himself as a faithful Jew. He was raised among his own people, trained as a Pharisee, the strictest party. He has not abandoned Israel's faith. He is on trial, he says, for holding on to it.

What is ‘the promise that God made to our fathers’? Paul means the hope running through Israel's Scriptures: that God would send his Messiah, restore his people, and raise the dead. ‘Our twelve tribes’ is a way of speaking of all Israel, worshipping and waiting together.

Then comes the sharp question: ‘Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?’ The Pharisees believed God would raise the dead at the end of the age. Paul's claim is that God has already begun, by raising Jesus. For a Jew who believed in the resurrection, why should that be impossible to believe? And for a Gentile like Festus, Paul is pressing a deeper question: if God is God, why should raising the dead be beyond him?
passages.ot: The promise to the fathers goes back to Abraham: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). The hope of the resurrection is in the Prophets: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise” (Isaiah 26:19), and “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake” (Daniel 12:2). The God who gives life is the God of Hannah's song: “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6).
passages.asks: Paul asked, ‘Why would any of you consider it incredible that God raises the dead?’ Ask what you find hardest to believe about God, and whether the God who made the world could do it. And ask whether your faith is a living hope, as Paul's was, or a set of ideas you agree with.

passages.happening: Paul admits that he too was once convinced he should do everything he could “to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth” (verse 9). In Jerusalem, with authority from the chief priests, he put many believers in prison, and when they were condemned to death he cast his vote against them (verse 10). He often had them punished in the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme. In his raging fury he even chased them to foreign cities (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is the fullest account in Acts of what Paul did before he met Jesus, and it is told by Paul himself. He does not spare himself. Prison. Death sentences. Punishment in the synagogues. Trying to force believers to ‘blaspheme’, to speak against Jesus. ‘Raging fury’.

‘I cast my vote against them’ has puzzled readers. Some think it means Paul was a member of the Sanhedrin and voted in its trials. Others think it is a way of saying he approved of their deaths, as he did at Stephen's stoning (8:1). Luke does not say which.

Why tell all this to a king? Because it is the honest truth, and because it makes his change hard to explain away. Paul was not a man looking for a new faith. He was the fiercest enemy of the one he now preaches. Something had to stop him.
passages.ot: Paul's zeal against the believers is the zeal he described before the crowd in Jerusalem (22:3-5), like the zeal of Phinehas: “he was zealous for his God” (Numbers 25:13). But the Scriptures also warn how a man can be sure he is serving God while he is fighting him. The Proverbs say, “There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death” (Proverbs 14:12).
passages.asks: Paul told a king and a governor the worst thing he had ever done. Ask whether you can be that honest about your own past when you tell what God has done for you. And Paul had been completely sure he was right. Ask whether there is anything you are completely sure of that you have never been willing to examine.

passages.t: ‘It is hard for you to kick against the goads’
passages.happening:
On his way to Damascus with the chief priests' authority, about noon, Paul saw “a light from heaven, brighter than the sun” shining around him and his companions (verses 12-13). They all fell to the ground, and he heard a voice say to him in Hebrew, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads” (verse 14).

He asked who was speaking. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” the Lord replied (verse 15). Then Jesus told him to get up, because he had appeared to him to appoint him a servant and a witness (verse 16). He would rescue him from his own people and from the Gentiles, and send him to them (verse 17) “to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God”, that they might receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those made holy by faith in Jesus (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is the third telling of Paul's turning in Acts. The note on Acts 9:1-9 sets out how the three tellings differ and how readers account for it. Here Paul tells it to a king, and he tells it short: Ananias is not mentioned, and Jesus's commission comes in one speech on the road. Many readers see the commission as coming from Jesus himself, even if Ananias later passed part of it on (9:15; 22:14-15).

Only this telling has the words ‘It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ A goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen. An ox that kicked back at it only hurt itself. ‘To kick against the goads’ was a Greek proverb for resisting a power you cannot escape; it appears in plays by the Greek writers Aeschylus and Euripides. Paul says Jesus spoke to him in Hebrew, yet he quotes a saying his Greek-speaking hearers would know at once. The point is plain. Paul was fighting God, and only hurting himself.

The task Jesus gave him gathers words from Isaiah: opening eyes, turning people from darkness to light. Paul presents his mission as the mission of Israel's Servant, a light for the nations. He is sent to his own people and to the Gentiles both.
passages.ot:
The commission echoes the Servant passages of Isaiah. God told his Servant, “I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind” (Isaiah 42:6-7). And, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

‘Get up and stand on your feet’ is how God called Ezekiel: “stand up on your feet and I will speak to you” (Ezekiel 2:1). And the promise of rescue is the one God gave Jeremiah: “Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you” (Jeremiah 1:8).
passages.asks: Jesus told Paul that he was only hurting himself by fighting. Ask whether there is any place where you are kicking against God's goad: resisting what you know he is asking. And the task Jesus gave Paul was to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light. Ask whose eyes you might help to open, by what you say and how you live.

passages.t: ‘I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision’
passages.happening:
“So then, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision” (verse 19). He preached first in Damascus and Jerusalem, then through Judea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent, turn to God, and show it by their deeds (verse 20). That is why he was seized in the temple and nearly killed (verse 21).

But he has had God's help to this day, and he testifies to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would happen (verse 22): “that the Christ would suffer, and as the first to rise from the dead, would proclaim light to our people and to the Gentiles” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
‘I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision.’ This is the summary of Paul's whole life since that noon on the road. He had been given a task, and he did it, at great cost.

His message was simple: repent, turn to God, and live in a way that shows it. ‘Repent’ means to change your mind and turn around. Paul did not preach a faith without fruit. Real turning shows in what a person does.

And once more he insists that his message is the message of Israel's Scriptures. The Christ, the Messiah, would suffer. He would be the first to rise from the dead. And he would bring light ‘to our people and to the Gentiles’. Paul says ‘our people’. Even now, on trial because of the leaders of his nation, he counts himself one of them, and the light is for them first.

He speaks ‘to small and great alike’. In this room there were a king, a princess and a governor, but Paul gives them the same message he gave to slaves and jailers.
passages.ot: The suffering of the Christ is in Isaiah's Servant song: “After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied” (Isaiah 53:11). The first to rise is foreshadowed in the Psalm Peter quoted at Pentecost: “nor will You let Your Holy One see decay” (Psalm 16:10). And the light for both Israel and the nations is Isaiah's promise again (Isaiah 49:6).
passages.asks: Paul could look back and say he had not been disobedient to what God showed him. Ask what God has shown you that you have not yet obeyed. And ask whether your faith shows in deeds ‘worthy of repentance’, things people around you could actually see.

passages.t: Festus: ‘You are insane’, and Agrippa's reply
passages.happening:
At this point Festus shouts, “You are insane, Paul! Your great learning is driving you to madness!” (verse 24). Paul answers, “I am not insane, most excellent Festus; I am speaking words of truth and sobriety” (verse 25). The king knows about these things, he says, and none of it escaped his notice, “because it was not done in a corner” (verse 26). “King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know you do” (verse 27).

Agrippa replies, “Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?” (verse 28). Paul answers that, short time or long, he prays to God that not only the king but everyone listening might become what he is, “except for these chains” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Festus interrupts when Paul reaches the resurrection. To an educated Roman, a dead man rising was nonsense. Many Greeks and Romans could believe the soul lived on, but a body raised from the grave seemed absurd, as the mockers at Athens showed (17:32). To Festus, Paul's learning has tipped into madness.

Paul answers calmly and politely. His words are ‘truth and sobriety’, sober good sense. And this was ‘not done in a corner’. Jesus's death, the empty tomb, the growth of the church in Jerusalem: all of it happened in public, in a city Agrippa's family knew well. A king who oversaw the temple could hardly have missed it.

Then Paul turns to the king: ‘Do you believe the prophets? I know you do.’ It is a clever and difficult question. If Agrippa says no, he denies the Scriptures before his own people. If he says yes, Paul will show him where the prophets lead.

Agrippa's reply is hard to translate. The Greek words can be taken in more than one way. Older English Bibles have ‘Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian’, as if the king were nearly won. Many modern Bibles, like the Berean Standard Bible, take it as ‘in such a short time’, and many readers hear a dry, perhaps mocking, tone: do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly? Others think the king is more serious than that, and is turning the question aside without saying no. Scholars do not agree, and these notes do not choose. Either way, Agrippa does not answer Paul's question about the prophets.

‘Christian’ is one of only three places the name appears in the New Testament (with 11:26 and 1 Peter 4:16). It seems to have begun as outsiders' word for the followers of Christ.

Paul's answer is one of the warmest lines in Acts. He wishes everyone in the room could become what he is. Then he lifts his chained hands: ‘except for these chains’.
passages.ot:
Prophets have often been called mad. When a young prophet came to anoint Jehu, the officers asked, “Why did this madman come to you?” (2 Kings 9:11). And the message of the prophets was not hidden: God says through Isaiah, “I have not spoken in secret, from a place in a land of darkness” (Isaiah 45:19).

Paul's longing for his hearers is like Jeremiah's: the word was “a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones” (Jeremiah 20:9), and he could not hold it in.
passages.asks: Festus called Paul mad, and Agrippa turned the question aside. Ask how you respond when someone presses the claims of Jesus on you personally. And Paul wished that everyone who heard him could have what he had, though not his chains. Ask whether you want that for the people around you, and whether they could tell.

passages.happening: The king rises, with the governor, Bernice and those sitting with them (verse 30). As they leave, they say to one another, “This man has done nothing worthy of death or imprisonment” (verse 31). And Agrippa says to Festus, “This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
The verdict is unanimous. The king, the governor and their advisers all agree: Paul is innocent. Luke has recorded the same verdict from the Roman commander (23:29) and from Festus (25:25), just as in his Gospel Pilate three times found no basis for a charge against Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

‘This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar.’ It is one of the strange turns of the story. Paul is innocent, and he still sails to Rome in chains. Was the appeal a mistake? Most readers do not think so. Paul appealed because Festus was ready to send him back to Jerusalem, where men had sworn to kill him. And the Lord had told him he must testify in Rome (23:11). Now he will, at the empire's expense, under the empire's guard, and before the emperor's court.

Luke does not say what Festus wrote in his letter to Nero. But the reader knows: the men who examined Paul found nothing.
passages.ot: God's plans have often gone forward through decisions that looked like loss. Joseph said to his brothers, “what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good” (Genesis 50:20). And the Proverbs say, “Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail” (Proverbs 19:21).
passages.asks: Paul was innocent and could have gone free, and instead he went to Rome in chains, where God had told him he must go. Ask whether you can trust God with a choice that, looking back, seems to have cost you. And ask whether you are able to see a purpose larger than your own freedom or comfort.
